title: Call flows that operators actually trace
summary: The ACK split, route sets, PRACK, UPDATE, session timers, teardown, and transfer.

lessons.title: Two different ACK rules
lessons.summary: The ACK for a non-2xx is hop by hop inside the INVITE transaction, and the ACK for a 2xx is a new end-to-end transaction.
objectives: Reuse the INVITE branch only for a non-2xx ACK
Send a 2xx ACK end to end with a new branch
Keep the CSeq number and change the method token to ACK

illustration.title: Which ACK is this?
illustration.caption: Look at the status code first, then the branch.
rows: UAC transaction user, end to end
ACK is still end to end

paragraphs: A final response from 300 through 699 is acknowledged by the INVITE client transaction. That ACK uses the INVITE's branch, the INVITE's CSeq number, and the method token ACK. Each hop generates its own ACK. A proxy does not forward the caller's ACK downstream.

The ladder below is that case. The proxy ACKs the peer with branch z9hG4bKproxy01, the same branch it put on the forwarded INVITE. The caller ACKs the proxy with branch z9hG4bKalice01. Neither ACK is a new transaction.

The ACK for a 200 OK is sent by the UAC using the dialog route set and the remote target. It carries a new branch because it is a different transaction. The CSeq number still matches the INVITE. Proxies that record-routed forward this ACK as they would any other mid-dialog request.

RFC 3261's overview describes INVITE as a three-way handshake, and that sentence is too small for the 2xx case. RFC 6026 corrects the state machine so a late 2xx is absorbed by the transaction, while the ACK remains the UAC's end-to-end request. The UAS retransmits the 200 OK until that ACK arrives.

fault.symptom: A proxy generates an ACK toward the caller for a 200 OK and never forwards the caller's ACK. The UAS keeps retransmitting 200 OK.

To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=314159

A 200 OK is acknowledged like a 603

lessons.title: Record-Route and the route set
lessons.summary: A proxy that wants to stay on the dialog prepends a Record-Route URI, and that URI has to contain lr.
objectives: Build the UAC route set by reversing Record-Route
Build the UAS route set in Record-Route order
Require lr on every Record-Route a proxy inserts

illustration.title: Who is first on the way back
illustration.caption: The proxy next to the caller ends up as the caller's first Route after the reverse.

layers.name: Request at the peer
layers.detail: Top Record-Route is the proxy next to the peer

layers.name: ACK Request-URI
layers.detail: The remote Contact, not the proxy

paragraphs: A proxy that wants later dialog requests inserts a Record-Route before any Record-Route already on the request. The URI is a sip or sips URI and it MUST contain lr. The UAS copies those values into the response in the same order.

The UAS route set is the request's Record-Route list in that order, so the proxy beside the UAS is first. The UAC route set is the response's Record-Route list in reverse order, so the proxy beside the UAC is first. The remote target is the Contact, and that becomes the Request-URI of the ACK.

With lr, each hop removes a top Route that names itself and forwards toward the next Route, leaving the Request-URI as the remote target. A missing lr falls into the older strict-routing procedure, which rewrites the Request-URI.

On this ladder the peer sees Core and then Edge. The caller reverses that into Edge and then Core. The ACK's first Route is 203.0.113.20. Edge will pop that Route and forward the ACK toward 198.51.100.30.

lessons.title: PRACK and reliable provisionals
lessons.summary: A provisional response with Require: 100rel is retransmitted until PRACK, and RAck names that exact response.
objectives: Offer 100rel and answer with RSeq
Build RAck from RSeq and the INVITE CSeq
Give PRACK its own CSeq number

illustration.title: RAck fields
illustration.caption: The first number is the provisional. The next two name the INVITE, not the PRACK.

paragraphs: RFC 3262 adds the option tag 100rel. The UAC puts it in Supported, or in Require when it will not proceed without reliable provisionals. The UAS sends the provisional with Require: 100rel and an RSeq number.

Until PRACK arrives, the UAS retransmits that provisional. 100 Trying is not made reliable this way. The responses you will see with RSeq are 180 and 183. Early media SDP in a 183 is reliable only after the PRACK succeeds.

PRACK uses a new branch and the next CSeq number in the dialog. RAck carries three tokens: the RSeq, the CSeq number of the request being acknowledged, and that request's method. For the first INVITE that is RAck: 1 1 INVITE when RSeq is 1.

The UAS answers PRACK with 200 OK and CSeq 2 PRACK. That 200 is not the INVITE's final response. The INVITE transaction is still open until its own final response, and the ACK rules for that final response are unchanged.

lessons.title: UPDATE before the INVITE completes
lessons.summary: UPDATE can change the session while the initial INVITE is still outstanding, and it does not use the ACK rules.
objectives: Send UPDATE only when no offer is outstanding
Treat UPDATE as a non-INVITE transaction
Keep dialog identifiers stable across the session change

illustration.title: Offer, answer, then a new offer
illustration.caption: The INVITE offer is answered in the 183. UPDATE is the next offer. The INVITE is still open.

paragraphs: RFC 3311 defines UPDATE. It can be sent in an early dialog, before the initial INVITE transaction completes, and it can be sent again after the dialog is confirmed. Success is 200 OK. There is no ACK for UPDATE.
UPDATE uses the next CSeq number and a new branch. Call-ID and both tags stay the same. That is the dialog. Changing the session description does not mint a new dialog id.

If the INVITE carried an offer, wait until that answer has been sent and, when 100rel is in use, acknowledged, before UPDATE carries another offer. Two offers outstanding at once is not a legal offer/answer exchange.

An SDP-only UPDATE changes the session. It is not the target-refresh procedure. Changing the remote target URI is covered by RFC 6141, and the mid-dialog request that operators use for that change is the re-INVITE. Read 6141 before you treat a new Contact as harmless.

lessons.title: Session-Expires and 422
lessons.summary: Session timers name who refreshes the dialog, and 422 tells the caller the interval was below Min-SE.
objectives: Read Session-Expires and the refresher parameter
Retry after 422 using the Min-SE from the response
Refresh with re-INVITE or UPDATE before the interval ends

illustration.title: Timer headers
illustration.caption: Min-SE is a floor. The absolute minimum in the specification is 90 seconds.
rows: Lowest interval this UA will accept
Ask again with a higher floor

paragraphs: RFC 4028 adds Session-Expires and Min-SE. The interval is in seconds. The refresher parameter is uac or uas and names who will send the refresh. Supported: timer means the UA can do this. Require: timer means the other side must.

Min-SE MUST NOT be lower than 90 seconds. A request may still be too small for the peer. The peer then answers 422 Session Interval Too Small and includes the Min-SE it will accept. That 422 is a non-2xx final response, so it is acknowledged inside the INVITE transaction.

The UAC retries with Session-Expires at least as large as the received Min-SE, and it raises its own Min-SE to that value. If the UAC asked to be the refresher and the UAS agrees, the 200 OK repeats refresher=uac.

The refresher sends a re-INVITE or an UPDATE before the interval expires. If the refresh does not happen, the UA treats the session as finished and sends BYE. The refresh is ordinary dialog work. It does not create a new Call-ID.

lessons.title: CANCEL, BYE, and re-INVITE
lessons.summary: CANCEL abandons an unanswered INVITE, BYE ends a confirmed dialog, and re-INVITE changes a dialog that already exists.
objectives: Pair 200 OK for CANCEL with 487 for the INVITE
Use BYE only on a confirmed dialog
Treat a mid-dialog INVITE as a re-INVITE and a possible target refresh

illustration.title: Three requests people mix up
illustration.caption: The dialog state decides the method. The branch decides whether CANCEL matches.
rows: 200 for CANCEL, 487 for INVITE, then ACK
The other INVITE is still open

paragraphs: CANCEL uses the same Request-URI, Call-ID, From, To, and CSeq number as the INVITE, and the same branch. The method token is CANCEL. It applies only while that INVITE has no final response. The UAS answers 200 OK to the CANCEL.

If the UAS stops the INVITE, the INVITE's final response is 487 Request Terminated. That 487 is a non-2xx, so the ACK reuses the INVITE branch. A 200 OK to CANCEL means the CANCEL was received. It does not mean the INVITE is already dead.

sections.h: BYE and re-INVITE need the dialog
paragraphs: BYE is sent only in a confirmed dialog, with both tags and a higher CSeq. If a 200 OK to the INVITE crosses the CANCEL, the dialog is confirmed and CANCEL will not tear it down. Send BYE.

A re-INVITE is a mid-dialog INVITE with a new CSeq. It can carry a new offer. If it changes the remote target in Contact, it is a target refresh and RFC 6141 is the document to read. A 491 Request Pending means the other side has an INVITE outstanding. Wait a short randomized time, as section 14 describes, and retry so the two requests do not collide again.

lessons.title: REFER and Replaces
lessons.summary: REFER asks another UA to send a request, and Replaces names the dialog that request should take over.
objectives: Read Refer-To and the 202 Accepted
Follow progress in NOTIFY sipfrag bodies
Match a Replaces dialog by Call-ID and both tags

illustration.title: Attended transfer
illustration.caption: REFER stays in the original dialog. The INVITE it causes is a new dialog that names the old one.

layers.name: REFER
layers.detail: Refer-To carries the target and the Replaces parameter
The REFER was accepted, not the new call

layers.name: INVITE
layers.detail: Replaces names call-id, to-tag, and from-tag

layers.name: NOTIFY
layers.detail: sipfrag reports how that INVITE is going

paragraphs: RFC 3515 defines REFER. Refer-To is the URI the recipient should request. Referred-By names who asked. The compact forms are r and b. The immediate response is 202 Accepted, which means the request to try was accepted.

The recipient then sends NOTIFY with Event: refer. The body is a sipfrag, a status line such as SIP/2.0 200 OK, showing how the referred request is progressing. 202 is not that result. You have to read the NOTIFY.

RFC 3891 defines Replaces. An attended transfer puts the dialog id into the Refer-To URI as a Replaces parameter, escaped. The UA that receives the resulting INVITE sees a Replaces header with call-id, to-tag, and from-tag.

Those three values are the same dialog identity you already use. If they match a confirmed dialog, the UA accepts the new INVITE and ends the replaced dialog. The early-only parameter limits Replaces to an early dialog. A mismatch is a failed replace, not a new unrelated call you should guess at.

fault.title: Transfer marked done at 202
fault.symptom: A tool closes the transfer when it sees 202 Accepted. The NOTIFY sipfrag later says SIP/2.0 486 Busy Here.
fault.log:
SIP/2.0 202 Accepted
CSeq: 2 REFER

NOTIFY
Event: refer
Content-Type: message/sipfrag

SIP/2.0 486 Busy Here
choices: 202 only accepts the REFER. The sipfrag is the referred call's result
486 means the REFER header was compact
fault.why: The subscription exists so the transferor can see failure as well as success.
fault.cause: The tool treated 202 as the target's final response.
fault.fix: Display the sipfrag status from NOTIFY. Keep the original dialog up until that result is final.
